title: Cat-Like Whiskers Help Tiny Drones Fly in the Dark
gist: Delft University of Technology researchers gave a palm-sized drone two 8-inch nickel-titanium whiskers so it can navigate walls, including glass, without vision, running the whole perception pipeline on 34 KB of memory. After a drift-correction algorithm, false positives fell from 38% to 0%, and the drone found a 2.5-foot exit in 90% of glass-room tests.

themes.theme: The problem: sensing in the dark

insights.claim: Ultra-compact search-and-rescue drones, lighter than a stick of butter, have limited compute and power, so cameras and lidar fail in smoke or darkness and may not detect even a clear pane of glass.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: The size needed to reach collapsed structures is the same constraint that disables conventional sensors, creating a niche for touch-based navigation.

insights.claim: Delft researchers took inspiration from nocturnal animals like mice and cats to build a lightweight tactile whisker sensor, based on Hamaza's view that touch sensing must be 'lightweight, low-latency, and low-power'.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Biomimetic tactile sensing is a low-cost complement to vision for micro-robots.
insights.quote: For tactile sensing to work on drones, it needs to be lightweight, low-latency, and low-power

insights.claim: The whiskers are 0.4 mm nickel-titanium wires, nearly 8 inches long (longer than the palm-sized drone), with three pressure sensors at each base that read wire bending to estimate distance and position of barriers.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Passive, cheap hardware substitutes for power-hungry sensors on tiny platforms.

insights.claim: Whisker drag on a wall could rotate and crash the drone, so across 72 flights at six angles and three speeds, 30, 45 and 60 degrees flew safely and 45 degrees was chosen for least orientation deviation, since 60 degrees reduces forward sensing range.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Mechanical integration, not just sensing, was the hard part for a flying whisker design.
insights.locator: The researchers compared a total of 72 flights

insights.claim: Even after filtering propeller vibration noise about 38 percent of detections were false positives, which the team traced to sensor drift and cut to 0 percent with a correction algorithm that estimates drift continuously in flight.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Software drift compensation, not better hardware, closed the reliability gap.
insights.locator: The researchers also encountered several hurdles

insights.claim: The drone flew parallel to transparent walls at 60-100 mm and could handle angled walls, which a drone with laser sensors would not manage.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Touch handles transparent obstacles that defeat optical sensing, a real capability edge.

insights.claim: With a probabilistic exploration method prioritizing unexplored areas, the drone found a 2.5-foot-wide exit in a small glass-walled room in 90 percent of tests, though real rubble is far less tidy than the lab setup.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Results remain lab-scale; the gap to cluttered disaster settings is the key commercialization risk.

insights.claim: The entire tactile perception pipeline runs onboard in 34 KB of a 192 KB memory budget with no external computer, per doctoral student Chao-Shan Ye.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: Tiny compute footprint leaves headroom for combining touch with other sensing on micro-drones.
insights.quote: Our entire tactile perception pipeline runs onboard using just 34 KB of memory
